prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.

Do not delay lumbar puncture or antibiotics to obtain a CT head: cranial imaging is not routine before lumbar puncture (WHO 2025 section A.4; NICE NG240 1.4.6) and no imaging-first criterion is present.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).
Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of age over 60 and diabetes mellitus (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.6.6).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 12, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose with paired blood glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: penicillin MIC 0.06 mg/L is susceptible by CLSI meningitis breakpoints, so benzylpenicillin or continued ceftriaxone for Streptococcus pneumoniae; stop ampicillin.
ENT assessment for drainage of the right ethmoid and maxillary sinus source and of the bony defect in the ethmoid roof, with follow-up for CSF rhinorrhoea and recurrent meningitis.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation). Compare with his known right-sided hearing loss.

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis.
No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 12, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycaemia.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

Bone erosion of the ethmoid roof next to the anterior cranial fossa is a direct route of spread: it calls for contrast MRI with venography to exclude subdural empyema, abscess and venous sinus thrombosis, ENT source control, and follow-up for CSF leak and recurrence.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild hyponatraemia is common in acute bacterial meningitis (inappropriate ADH secretion, or volume depletion from vomiting and fever, as the raised urea suggests); it is a complication of the illness, not an alternative explanation. red_herrings.intended_effect: Redirect workup toward primary endocrine or volume-status causes of hyponatremia.

clinical_pearls: The classic triad of fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status is present in only 44% of bacterial meningitis cases, but at least two of four symptoms (headache, fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status) are present in 95%
Jolt accentuation of headache (worsening with rapid horizontal rotation of the head) supports meningitis when present, but a negative test does not exclude it
S. pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults, accounting for approximately 50% of cases
Do not delay antibiotics for any reason: mortality rises with each hour of delay in antibiotic administration
Adjunctive dexamethasone is started shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose (WHO 2025; NICE NG240)

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Javier Herrera is a 62-year-old right-handed man with a history of type 2 diabetes, chronic sinusitis, and mild right-sided hearing loss who presents to the emergency department via ambulance with approximately 12 hours of progressively worsening headache, fever, and altered mental status. His wife reports that he came home from work yesterday evening around 5 PM complaining of a severe, rapidly worsening diffuse headache, throbbing in character. He took ibuprofen 600 mg without relief. Over the ensuing hours, he developed shaking chills and his wife measured a temperature of 102.8°F (39.3°C) at 9 PM. He went to bed early but was restless and moaning throughout the night. By 3 AM, his wife noticed he was confused and not making sense when she tried to talk to him. He was complaining that the bedroom light was too bright and kept his eyes closed. He vomited twice between 3 AM and 5 AM, which was non-bloody and non-bilious. She called 911 at approximately 5:15 AM when she could not fully rouse him and he did not recognize their children. EMS found him febrile at 39.5°C with a heart rate of 122 and blood pressure of 148/82. He was transported emergently. In the ED, he is lethargic, photophobic, and in obvious distress. He is intermittently groaning and reaching for his head. Notably, the patient had been treated for an acute sinusitis exacerbation approximately 10 days ago with a course of amoxicillin-clavulanate, which he completed 3 days prior to this presentation. His wife denies any recent head trauma, seizure activity, rash, ear discharge, or known sick contacts with meningitis. She confirms his immunizations are up to date, though she is uncertain about meningococcal vaccination.
